Course 07

Reading studies without getting lost

Correlation, causation, samples and results.

Lesson 2. Samples and generalisation

1 · Lesson

No study can observe everyone, so it works with a sample. The key question is: whom does that sample represent? A study with 40 psychology students from one university says something about those people, but perhaps not about retirees in another country.

In 2010, Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan pointed out that most psychological research was done with people from WEIRD societies (Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic), who are not representative of humanity. Some results thought to be universal turned out to vary across cultures.

Size also matters: with small samples, results fluctuate a lot by chance, and it is easier to find effects that later fail to replicate. A large sample guarantees nothing if it is biased, but a small one calls for caution.

2 · Example

The Müller-Lyer illusion (two equal lines that look different in length because of the arrows at their ends) was considered universal. In classic studies with populations from different cultures, the strength of the illusion varied greatly between groups. Perception also has a learned component.

3 · Activity

Find a news item about a psychology study. Find out how many people took part, from which country and of what age. To whom do you think its conclusions apply, and to whom not?
